s16.slug: THURSDAY · 10:05 PM · MISSION STREET, OUTSIDE THE WALGREENS
body: Four blocks east of Bastille the Walgreens has every light in it on. From the curb the store shows through the front windows end to end, like a drugstore somebody built for a museum: the photo counter with its gate down, the aisle of tinsel and Scotch tape, the cashier in her tinsel headband stacking eggnog cartons into a pyramid by the door. On the Christmas endcap somebody has filled the hook with gold-foil coins again.
The cashier looks up from the pyramid and sees him through the glass, and lifts a carton at him, a little, the way you’d wave at somebody you can’t place.

Out here the sidewalk is empty both ways to the lights. Bastille is four blocks behind him with its string lights and the bell on its door and everybody he knows inside it. His ears still have the room in them.
He opens the RAZR.
He shuts it on Laney. He opens it again and goes down the list to SKYE (MISFIT), and stands there in the light from the store with his thumb on the green key.

She has called him from her mother’s balcony in Studio City, and from a parking garage three floors under it, and from a laundromat at one in the morning with a dress going around in the suds. In three weeks he hasn’t asked her for one thing.
He presses it. She picks up on the second ring. Behind her a screen door is banging somewhere, and farther off than that there’s surf.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her hand went for the bell and found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. ‘You stayed. She wanted you here.’

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window.

choices.text: “Can you come get me?”
response: “Can you come get me?”

response.text: “You called,” Skye says, and leaves it at that.

response: “Where are you.”
“Mission. The Walgreens.”
Keys, already, on her end. “Eleven minutes.”

choices.text: “Is the offer to go nowhere still open?”
response: “Is the offer to go nowhere still open?”
“It’s always open,” Skye says. “That’s what nowhere *is*.” And quicker, with keys in it: “Where are you.”
He tells her. “Eleven minutes,” she says.

choices.text: “Where are you?”
response: “Where are you?”
“Up north. I said.” The screen door again, closer, and her bare feet on boards. “Where are *you*.”
He tells her. And then she’s coming.

s16a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:16 PM · THE SAAB, MISSION STREET → DEL PLAYA
body: Eleven minutes later the Saab comes down Mission with its top down at forty-three degrees, the only car on the street, and noses in at the curb under the drugstore’s glare. She’s in the gray Marisol sweatshirt from the launch ramp, with the price tag gone from the cuff, and her feet are bare on the pedals.

He gets in. She doesn’t put it in gear. She looks at him, at his face in that light, while the signal at the corner goes green and yellow and red and green again over an empty street, and she reads it to the bottom. When she’s done she reaches across him and turns the heater over to the floor on his side, onto his boots, and puts the car in gear.

At the first light he takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt and holds the red key down. It plays its little falling chime, four notes going downstairs, and the screen goes black in his hand. Skye hears it. Her eyes go to his hand and back to the light, which is green, and she drives.

*Two in the morning, and a car, and nobody who knows where you are.* Father Osei said it on Saturday, through the linen. It’s a quarter past ten, and it’s a car, and nobody knows where he is, and seven hours ago he had her in daylight on a trunk lid with pencils rolling off it and it was easy. He knows which kind of hour this is. He sits back in the seat and lets her drive it.
Mission runs out at the Grove. At the last light, with the eucalyptus black on both sides of the road, Skye says it to the windshield.
“I told you I don’t take people home.”
“I remember.”
“I’ve decided I want to.”

She turns west into Las Olas. Del Playa on a Thursday night at half past ten is music out of three houses at once, a couch on somebody’s lawn with two people asleep on it sitting up, a kid on a roof with a flashlight looking for something in the gutter. She doesn’t park on it. She takes the alley behind, and stops the Saab nose-in beside a trash can with a house number painted on it in nail polish, and they go around to the front through a side yard grown over with ice plant.

The house is two stories of shingle gone silver, with a porch across the front that leans toward the street like it’s trying to hear something. On the porch stands a surfboard rack built out of two-by-fours, with no surfboards on it. “They’re in Baja,” she says. “The boys. Sol’s in LA. It’s just me and the darkroom.”

Inside, off the hall, there’s a door with a towel rolled along the bottom of it and a red bulb over the frame, unlit, and a smell of vinegar coming out from under the towel. She goes past it and starts up the stairs ahead of him, barefoot.
Halfway up she turns around on the stair, above him, with her hand on the rail. “This is where I’m going to live,” she says. “In January. When I’m normal.”

s17.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: Her room is lit by its window. She strung the Christmas lights around the frame herself — there’s a thumbtack every foot, and where she ran out of thumbtacks, gaff tape — and the left half of the strand is out, so the right half throws red and green and a white gone yellow down onto a mattress on a low frame under the sill, and the left half throws nothing at all. The window is open a few inches at the bottom. Through it come the surf at the foot of the bluff and somebody’s stereo three houses down, taking turns.

A clothes rack on casters is most of the furniture: flannels, a black dress in plastic, a parka for somewhere colder than California, and under it a row of boots lined up heel to heel. Scripts in rubber bands stand in a stack against the wall, the brads winking. By the bed there’s a jar of beach glass, green and brown, with one blue piece set on top last. There’s nothing on the walls. “Walls are for leases,” she says, when she sees him look. Nothing in this room knows anything about him but her.

On the sill, under the working half of the lights, a paperback O’Connor lies open at the end of the story with its spine broken in two places, and he knows the margin before he’s close enough to read it: her capitals, and one hard line of Sharpie through CON.

On the back of the door, on the one hook, in a dry cleaner’s bag with a paper collar around the hanger, hangs a white dress with a collar that stands up and forty buttons down the front. “The top leaks,” Skye says. “I wasn’t leaving it in the car. Wardrobe gets it Monday.” He knows the dress. His body knows it faster than he does.

She turns him by the shoulders and peels the Carhartt down off his arms and hangs it on the hook over the dress, so the dress is gone under brown canvas that smells of the Anchor’s fryer. She looks at the white iPhone in her hand, at the time on it, and drops it into one of the boots under the rack.
“No clock tonight,” she says.
She kicks a heap of clothes in under the rack with one bare foot. “Housekeeping,” she says.
“You’re the first person up those stairs,” she says to the boot with the phone in it, “who wasn’t Sol, or a surfer looking for a towel.” And then she turns around.

She starts where the turnout left off. The sweatshirt comes off over her head and lands on the jar of beach glass, and there’s nothing under it, and she’s already at his shirt buttons from the top, fast, and shoving the shirt off his shoulders, and the undershirt after it, so they’re skin to skin standing up in the middle of the room in the light off the window, and cold for about the length of a breath. She walks him backward by his belt loops till the frame of the bed catches him behind the knees, and he goes down onto the mattress, and she comes down with him, and the frame says something about it in pine.

It’s the first time they’ve been lying down. Every other time there was a car around them, or a trailer bench, or a gearshift, or somebody’s knuckles on a door. Here there’s a mattress and a window and her weight, and she puts all of it on him.

She’s warm everywhere he’d have guessed and in places he wouldn’t — the backs of her arms, the small of her back — and cold only where the window gets her: one shoulder blade, the side of her face, which he warms with his hand. Her breasts against his chest. Her hair coming down around both their faces, gold where the lights get into it and stiff with salt at the ends. He learns her with his mouth: the hinge of her jaw, the hollow at the base of her throat where her pulse is going, the slope of her breast, and she arches into it and says something into his hair that hasn’t got words in it. Her mouth goes to his chest, his collarbone, the side of his neck under his ear. Her hands go down his ribs one at a time, as if she’s counting them for wardrobe.

“Since Monday,” she says against his mouth. “Since the trailer. I stood in the rain with a boy dripping on me for three takes and counted buttons all through them and kept getting forty-one.” She bites his lower lip, not gently. “I’m not counting anything tonight.”

Lying down, her mouth on his is a different thing: slower, heavier, nothing to brace against and nowhere either of them has to be. She kisses him like she’s reading something she means to know by heart, and goes back over the parts she likes. He has wanted this since a window seat in Montecito, and he lets himself know it.

“In a world,” she says against his ear, low and doomed, in the voice from every movie trailer ever cut, “where one man from Ohio —” her hand goes down his chest to his stomach “— wore a *belt* —” and loses it laughing into his neck, and doesn’t finish.

Her feet are cold, even now. She puts them on his shins on purpose and laughs into his neck when he jumps. He gets his hands into her hair and holds her face up where he can see it, with the red and the green of the lights in her eyes, and she lets him look for as long as she can stand it, and then she doesn’t.

At some point he rolls them, and she lets him, for about as long as it takes her to laugh at him for it; then she rolls them back, and the stack of scripts by the bed goes over and slides across the floor in its rubber bands, and they let it. She settles over him with her knees on either side of his hips and both hands spread on his chest, and looks down at him like she’s deciding where to start, and starts everywhere. Her skin tastes of salt, and faintly of oranges.

Reaching up past him to steady herself on the sill she knocks the Christmas lights, and the bulbs are warm against her arm, and one more of them gives out. “Oh, *come on*,” she tells it, and comes back down to him laughing.

Her earring catches in his hair — a small gold hoop — and pins his head to hers, and she stops everything to laugh, holding his head still in both hands while she works it loose. “Hold *still*. I’m stuck in you.” She gets it free, and kisses the place it pulled.

She says his name. Not *Jack*; all of it — *Jack Costigan* — low, in her own voice, looking down at him from a few inches away with the lights behind her head. He stops at the sound of it. She smiles, and puts her mouth back on his.
He wants her. No part of him is pretending otherwise, and she can feel that it isn’t, and he feels her smile about it against his throat.

body.text: He doesn’t want to be good right now. He knows it, and he knows he’s choosing, and he goes on choosing. Her mouth. The lights. Her hips on his through two layers of denim. Her hands going down his stomach to his belt, and he lets them, and the buckle gives, and the leather goes slack, and it’s a breath, and another breath, before the part of him that’s still awake gets its voice back.
body.else: Under all of it there’s a voice in him, quiet and clear, and it’s his own, and it has known where this was going since the alley. It isn’t loud. It doesn’t have to be. Her hands go down his stomach to his belt, quick and sure, and find the buckle, and there’s no question in them anywhere; she’s smiling against his mouth with the tongue of the buckle halfway out of its hole, and the voice says it.

choices.text: “No.”
choices.key: On her bed on Del Playa, with her hands at your belt, you said no. One word.
response: “No.”
Her hands stop. They come off the buckle all at once.
She laughs, one short laugh down at him. “That’s funny,” she says. “That’s a very funny —” She sees his face, and the laugh stops.
For a moment she just stays there above him, with her hair down around her face and her hands open in the air where the buckle was, like somebody who reached for a stair that wasn’t there.
“I didn’t *ask* you anything,” she says, as if that settles it. Then, slower, finding out that it doesn’t: “I didn’t think I had to.”

She sits back on her heels on the mattress. Her hair has come down on one side. She reaches over the edge of the bed for the man’s flannel on the floor by the rack, and pulls it on, and does up three buttons, the wrong three, and holds it shut at the throat with one fist.
“Oh,” she says. Her mouth has gone into a line he hasn’t seen on her before, straight across, holding something level.
And after a while, to the lit half of the window: “You can go. I’ll drive you. It’s fine.” She starts to get up to look for her keys.
His body hasn’t caught up with what he said. It’s still on the mattress a minute ago, and it lets him know.

He finds his undershirt in the sheets and pulls it on. His shirt he leaves where it landed, and the Carhartt on its hook. He sits down at the foot of the mattress, with his back against the clothes rack, so the hems of her flannels brush his shoulders.
She stops halfway off the bed and looks at him.
“I’m not going anywhere,” he says.
The fist at her throat lets go of the flannel.

Three houses down a party turns its music up, and somebody whoops, and it turns it down again. Skye sits back down. She draws her knees up inside the flannel and looks at him over them, with her arms locked around them and her fingers holding her own wrists hard enough that the knuckles have gone pale.
“Why?” she says. She sounds like she wants to know.

choices.text: “I want to. I’m not going to.”
choices.key: On her bed on Del Playa, with her hands at your belt, you told her you want to, and you’re not going to.

choices.key: On her bed on Del Playa you put your hand over hers on the buckle and said no.
response: He puts his hand over hers on the buckle. Her fingers are warm and quick under his, and they stop when his close on them. “Skye,” he says. “No.”
Her hand comes out from under his.
She laughs, one short laugh down at him. “That’s funny,” she says. “That’s a very funny —” She sees his face, and the laugh stops.
For a moment she just stays there above him, with her hair down around her face and her hands open in the air where the buckle was, like somebody who reached for a stair that wasn’t there.
“I didn’t *ask* you anything,” she says, as if that settles it. Then, slower, finding out that it doesn’t: “I didn’t think I had to.”

She sits back on her heels on the mattress. Her hair has come down on one side. She reaches over the edge of the bed for the man’s flannel on the floor by the rack, and pulls it on, and does up three buttons, the wrong three, and holds it shut at the throat with one fist.
“Oh,” she says. Her mouth has gone into a line he hasn’t seen on her before, straight across, holding something level.
And after a while, to the lit half of the window: “You can go. I’ll drive you. It’s fine.” She starts to get up to look for her keys.
His body hasn’t caught up with what he said. It’s still on the mattress a minute ago, and it lets him know.

He finds his undershirt in the sheets and pulls it on. His shirt he leaves where it landed, and the Carhartt on its hook. He sits down at the foot of the mattress, with his back against the clothes rack, so the hems of her flannels brush his shoulders.
She stops halfway off the bed and looks at him.
“I’m not going anywhere,” he says.
The fist at her throat lets go of the flannel.

Three houses down a party turns its music up, and somebody whoops, and it turns it down again. Skye sits back down. She draws her knees up inside the flannel and looks at him over them, with her arms locked around them and her fingers holding her own wrists hard enough that the knuckles have gone pale.
“Why?” she says. She sounds like she wants to know.

s18.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: Her laptop is open on the floor beside the beach glass, playing something slow and low: a woman’s voice worn soft at the edges, a piano under it, strings coming in behind. “So it isn’t so quiet in here,” Skye said, putting it on, and went back to her end of the bed.

She’s sitting against the wall at the head of the mattress in the flannel, with her knees up and the working half of the lights in her hair. He’s at the foot in his undershirt, his back against the clothes rack. Two mugs of mint tea she went downstairs and made at a quarter past eleven sit on the blanket, going cold in the same place. Whatever was in her face twenty minutes ago, she has put it somewhere. What’s there now is interest, sharp as a new pencil.
She hasn’t said *go* again. She’s been asking him things instead, quick, one after another, the way they run lines at a table read at four in the morning, and she wants every answer.
“What’s a mortal sin.”
“Something serious, that you know is serious, that you do anyway, on purpose. All three.”
“Who decides it’s serious?”
“The Church says what’s serious. Whether you knew, and meant it — that’s between you and God.”
“So it’s the honor system.”
“Pretty much.”
“Does it count if you’re not Catholic?”
“It counts different. You can’t be on the hook for a rule nobody ever gave you. That’s in the Catechism.” Near enough.
“What does your grandmother think happens to people who do it anyway?”
“She thinks they should go to confession.” He considers his grandmother. “And then eat something.”
“Is it the same rule for boys?”
“Same rule. Same nuns.”
“And did the nuns tell the boys?”
“Every Friday in Lent.”
She takes each answer and keeps it. He can see her keep them, one at a time.
“Is it a sin to want to?”
“No. Wanting’s not the sin. It’s what you do about it.”
“So you can want me as much as you like.”
“As much as I like.”
“And you do.”
“And I do.”
She’s pleased with that one; he can tell from her eyebrows. “And if you do it anyway? The thing.”
“You go and say so. You mean it. You try not to again.”
“And they let you back in?”
“Every time.”
“That’s a better deal than my industry,” she says. And then, not looking away from him: “When did you decide? Tonight? In the car?”
“A long time before tonight.”
“Before me.”
“Before you.”
“So it isn’t about me.”
“It’s about you too,” Jack says. “It isn’t because of you.”
She turns that over and puts it with the others.
At twenty to twelve she puts her tea down on the floor and wraps both arms around her knees.

“Real one,” she says. “Is it God? Does God care where your hands are? Because I’ve met a lot of men who say *God* and mean their mother. I went out with one for a summer. His mother called him during dessert.”
“And don’t tell me you don’t want to. I was *there*.”
She looks at him over her knees. “You threw a game for Him on a road full of cows. I thought it was a reflex.” She waits. “It isn’t, is it.”

choices.text: “Where my hands are is the small part. What I’d be saying is the big part. A body says things whether you mean it to or not.”
response: “Where my hands are is the small part,” Jack says. “What I’d be saying is the big part. A body says things whether you mean it to or not.”
“Says *what*?”
“That’s the next move.”
“You keep saying *move*. Is this a debate?”
“It’s a little bit a debate.”
“Good,” she says. “I win debates.” She wraps both hands around her tea, and looks at him over it like she has all night, which she does.

choices.text: “God cares where everybody’s hands are. It’s a big job. He delegates to grandmothers.”
response: “God cares where everybody’s hands are,” Jack says. “It’s a big job. He delegates to grandmothers.”
She laughs, and doesn’t let him off. “Funny. Answer it.”
So he tries. A body says things, he tells her, whether you mean it to or not. She narrows her eyes at that, and points her tea at him to keep going.
“And you’ll notice,” he says, “I answered it.”
“You answered it *second*,” Skye says. “Joke first. I know that move. I *invented* that move.”

choices.text: “I don’t know how to say it without sounding like a pamphlet.”
response: “I don’t know how to say it without sounding like a pamphlet.”
“Sound like a pamphlet. I’ll do the voice.”

And she does. She’s up on her knees on the mattress with an invisible guitar strap over one shoulder and her eyebrows up at her hairline, a youth minister at the end of a lock-in, after the trust falls and before the pizza. “So, guys. Real talk. Your body? Is a *temple*.” She checks the room for agreement. “And you don’t take a temple to the *drive-in*.”
She drops back against the wall. “Fine. Now you.”
So he tries, pamphlet and all, and she lets him. It comes out worse than the youth minister and truer, and somewhere in the middle of it she puts the invisible guitar down.

s18a.slug: FRIDAY · 12:50 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: An hour on, the song is long gone and the laptop has wandered off into other songs that she isn’t listening to and he can barely hear. She has had him on the Sixth Commandment, and on the Song of Songs, which she didn’t know was in the Bible and has pulled up on the laptop on her knees and is reading him out of, one finger on the screen. “*Your lips are like a scarlet strand.* This is in the *Bible*. You people have been holding out.” She scrolls. “*Your hair is like a flock of goats*? Jack. That’s a *compliment*?” She has had him on why priests can’t marry, and on whether his grandmother ever kissed anybody but his grandfather, which he has never asked and is never going to. She has had him on Saturdays.
“And what do you *say* in there?”
“The truth.”
“All of it?”
“That’s the deal.”
“Does the priest ever laugh?”
“One did. He was right to.”

“A body says things,” she says, somewhere in the hour, after he has tried it on her twice. “Fine. Mine’s been saying things for money since I was eleven. It says whatever’s on the page. It said *I’m saving myself* for three seasons on a lake, with a burrito in my trailer between takes.” She points her tea at him. “So don’t tell me a body can’t lie. It’s the best liar I’ve got.”
“That’s acting,” Jack says. “Everybody knows it’s acting. That’s the deal with acting.”
“And what’s the deal with this?”
“There isn’t a cut.”
She looks at him for that one a good while, and lets him have it, and goes back for more tea.
“Is it hard?” she says. “The not.”
“Yes.”
“How hard?”
“You were there.”
She considers that, and seems to find it fair.
She’s quiet for a minute over her tea. She sets it on the floor and comes forward onto her knees on the mattress, and he can see her bring the big one up from wherever she’s been keeping it.
“Same two people,” she says. “Same bed. Same everything. A man in a robe says some words over us, and then it’s *holy*, and tonight it’s a *sin*?” She leans in. “You’d make love to a notary.”

He laughs, and she doesn’t; she isn’t finished. “I’ve been to nine weddings in this business, Jack. Two of them were for green cards. One was for a network — they told the bride what to wear in a *meeting*. I’ve watched people say the words in front of four hundred people and a string quartet and go home to separate wings of the house. And I’ve seen two people in a makeup trailer at four in the morning, who never signed a thing in their lives, love each other so hard you had to go and wait outside.” She sits back on her heels. “I’ve signed a lot of paper. None of it ever meant I loved anybody. So tell me what the paper does.”

choices.text: “The paper’s the least of it. The promise is the thing. You don’t say forever with your body before you’ve said it with your life.”
response: “The paper’s the least of it,” Jack says. “The promise is the thing. You don’t say forever with your body before you’ve said it with your life.”
She waits, so he finishes it. “Otherwise your body’s lying. And I’m a bad enough liar with my mouth.”
“And if you say it and then you don’t keep it? People don’t. I’ve been to the weddings.”
“Then you go back and keep it again. That’s most of what keeping is.”
“Who says forever?”
“A Pope. John Paul the Second. Five years of Wednesdays on it.”
“People *went*?”
“Thousands.”
She looks up at the ceiling, considering the thousands. “I’d have gone once,” she says. “For the hats.”

choices.text: “I don’t know if I’ll get it right when it’s my turn. I just know I want it to be true the first time.”
response: “I don’t know if I’ll get it right when it’s my turn,” Jack says. “I just know I want it to be true the first time.”
“*First*,” Skye says.
She sits back against the wall with that, and the knees come up again inside the flannel, and for the first time tonight she hasn’t got the next question ready. Eventually she finds one.
“How will you know? When it’s your turn.”
“I won’t, probably. That’s the part I pray about.”
She looks at him like it’s either the dumbest thing she has heard all year or the bravest, and she’s going to need until morning to decide which.

choices.text: “Something happened when I was sixteen. I prayed like somebody was there. Somebody was.”
response: “Something happened when I was sixteen,” Jack says. “I prayed like somebody was there. Somebody was.”
She waits, so he finishes it. “Everything since is me trying to act like I believe that.”
“What’s it like?” she says. “Somebody being there.”
“Like getting caught,” Jack says. “And nobody making you leave.”
She doesn’t push. She asks once. “Is it your brother? The sixteen thing. You said sometime.”
“A fight,” Jack says, to the jar of beach glass. “A guy got hurt. Bad. My brother took five years.”
“Okay,” Skye says, and lets it be, and picks her tea back up.

s18v.slug: FRIDAY · 1:40 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM

body.text: She’s quiet a long time. On the floor the laptop moves on to another song and she doesn’t hear that one either. “Nobody’s ever told me a reason that wasn’t about *them*,” she says.

“That’s a good argument,” Skye says. “I hate it. Say it again so I can find the hole.” He says it again. She goes at it from the front, and from both ends, and from underneath, and can’t find it, and throws a pillow at him for that.
She laughs at the ceiling. “You’d have been a terrible actor.”
“I’d have been a great Bible salesman.”
“You’d have sold one,” she says. “To me.”

body: After that the talk goes wider, and gets away from him. Her mother’s legal pad, and the notes that come up with the coffee. His father’s garage in winter, with the space heater going and the Browns losing on the radio. The parrot in her mother’s kitchen, and what it says, and to whom. Which Brown he’d trade for a kicker who could make a short one. Whether the Saab will outlive the people who stopped making it. What she’d be if she couldn’t act, which she says is a first, being asked, and takes twenty minutes over. The first car she ever drove, at fourteen, on a backlot in Valencia, into a hedge that had been in a Western. The girl who played her big sister on a kids’ show, who sells houses in Tarzana now and is the happiest person Skye knows. Somewhere in it the laptop runs out of songs and goes to sleep on the floor with a small white light breathing on its front, and they leave it there.

s19.slug: FRIDAY · 3:30 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: By half past three the laptop is asleep and more of the strand has given up: the dark has come down the left side of the window and across the top, and what’s left of the lights runs down the right side and along the sill. Skye has turned on the mattress to face the wall. She’s sitting with her knees drawn up in the flannel and her back half to him.

She has talked for most of four hours, and for the last quarter of one she hasn’t. He’s at the foot of the bed against the clothes rack, where he sat down at twenty past eleven, with a script she handed him at two o’clock open on his knee — a pilot about a family that runs a motel in Reno, with her notes down the margins in the same downhill capitals — and he hasn’t turned a page since three.

When she does it’s to the wall. “I’ve been looked at for a living since I was eleven,” she says. “Everybody always wanted something. A face. A laugh on the take. A picture for the nephew.” The wall is plaster, with a crack running up it the shape of a river on a map. “And everything I’ve ever done with my body, with anybody, I did like somebody was watching. Like it was for the room.” A pause. “And you’re telling me it was *saying* something. All along.”

“My mother had a word for some of the girls I worked with,” she says. “Not that word. *Reputation*. *That one has a reputation.* She’d write it on the legal pad next to their names, like a height.” Her thumb finds the crack in the plaster. “I was always very careful not to have one where she could see.”

“People look at me and decide,” she says. “It’s fine. It’s the job. They decide, and I let them, and I know what they decided before they do.” She follows the crack up the wall with her thumb as far as she can reach. “Tonight you decided something, and I don’t know what it was. At twenty past eleven I thought I knew what it was. Then you sat down on my floor and didn’t leave, and I haven’t known since. So I’ve been very interested for four hours. I’m good at interested.”
She pulls the cuffs of the flannel down over her hands and holds them shut from the inside. Her eyes go to the window, to the dark half of it.
“Can I ask you something.”
“Yeah.”
“Do you think I’m a slut?”

She goes on, at the window. “Because I like you. A lot. And I care what you think. That doesn’t happen to me. I know what everybody thinks — that’s the job, knowing — but I don’t *care*. I care what you think.” She stops. “I don’t have a part for this.”
At the foot of the bluff the surf comes in and pulls the gravel back down with it, a long rattle, and comes in again.

Jack doesn’t answer her. He puts the script down on the floor, open, and comes up the mattress on his knees and gets his arms around her from the side — flannel, knees, the cuffs over her hands, all of her he can reach — with his chin by her hair.
The flannel smells of her and of somebody’s cedar closet. Under it her shoulders are all bone and held breath.
She goes stiff. He feels it down the length of her: her back hard against his chest under the flannel, her hands staying where they are inside the cuffs. She doesn’t lean.
“No,” he says, into her hair.
She doesn’t move.
“No. I don’t think anything like that about you. Not once. Not on the beach in November, not in your car, not tonight.”
That would be a good place to stop. She asked him straight, though, so he doesn’t.

“I’ll tell you the other true thing too,” he says. “I don’t like thinking about you with anybody else. Some guy in a trailer. Some guy in a pool house. I hate it, actually. Monday a guy who called me cuz all night stood in the rain with you for three takes, and that’s all he did, and I’d have liked to put him through the side of a Studebaker.” He hears how that sounds and leaves it sounding like that. “But that’s mine. That’s me being jealous. It’s about me. What I think about *you* is a different thing.”
She’s still stiff under his arms. He keeps them where they are.
The rest of it is further down, and he has to go and get it.

“The stuff the Church says about this,” he says. “Where your hands go. Who with. I was raised on it, and I was raised to use it on *me*. It’s for judging what I do. That’s what it’s for.” Her hair smells of the Saab and of pencil shavings. “Saturdays I go in with a list. It’s long, and every line on it is mine. I don’t bring anybody else’s. It isn’t my job to.”

“You want to know what’s on it this week? You aren’t. Me in your car is. Me in that trailer. Me tonight, before I said it.” He can feel her listening, all down her back. “My grandmother does it the other way round. She’s got a list for everybody on Glenwood Avenue, and once a month she goes to confession and tells the priest about the weather.”

“You can look at a thing and say it’s wrong. You’re allowed to. You’re supposed to, if somebody asks. But what a person is — you don’t get to decide that. That’s God’s to decide, and He’s a lot more merciful about it than I’d be.” He looked the words up once and kept them. “It’s in the Catechism, near enough. You can say a thing’s grave. The person, you leave to God — to His justice and His mercy. Both of them. It says both.”
He tightens his arms. “So when somebody asks, you tell them the truth about it, straight. You asked me. I did. And then you’re supposed to be hard on yourself and easy on everybody else.”
“I’m very good at the first part.”
It isn’t enough yet. He can feel that it isn’t, all down her back. He goes looking for the rest.

choices.text: Give her the participle.
choices.key: At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and told her she was worth something before anybody ever pointed a camera at her.

response.text: He gives her the rest of what the priest said on Tuesday, in his own words, since he hasn’t got the Greek.
response.else: He gives her the rest of what a friend texted him on Tuesday, in his own words, since he hasn’t got the Greek.

response: “That feast,” he says into her hair. “Full of grace before she’d done a single thing. I think that goes for everybody. Not the no-stain part. The first part. You were worth something before anybody ever pointed a camera at you. Before the lake. Before the legal pad —”

response.text: “You said that,” Skye says, to the wall. “At the laundromat.”

response: “Nothing you did makes you less than that. And nothing you do with me makes you more. I said no because of what you’re worth. Not because of anything you did.”
She’s quiet against him. “You’re going to make me cry on a Friday,” she says. “I don’t cry off the clock.”
“I’ll risk it.”
“You’re the only person who’s ever told me no and meant it,” Skye says. “Do you know what that does to a person?”
He doesn’t. He holds on.

She turns around inside his arms at last, flannel and cuffs and all, and puts her face in his neck. “I thought you’d hug me and not answer,” she says there. “That’s what nice people do. They hold you so they don’t have to say it.”
And she leans.

choices.text: Tell her you pray for her. By name.
choices.key: At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and told her you pray for her by name.
response: “I pray for you,” he says. “By name. Since the first candle.”
Under his arms she goes still in a different way. “You *pray* for me?”
“Every day.”
“What do you *say*?”
He tells her. Her name. Then whatever he’s got that day: that she’d be all right; that she’d sleep; one night in Youngstown, that she’d quit driving barefoot.
She laughs into her knees, a short breath of it. “Does it work?”
“I don’t know yet. You’re still driving barefoot.”
“I’m always going to drive barefoot.”
“I know. I keep asking.”
“You’re the only person who’s ever told me no and meant it,” Skye says. “Do you know what that does to a person?”
He doesn’t. He holds on.

She turns around inside his arms at last, flannel and cuffs and all, and puts her face in his neck. “I thought you’d hug me and not answer,” she says there. “That’s what nice people do. They hold you so they don’t have to say it.”
And she leans.

choices.text: The splinter and the beam.
choices.key: At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and told her about the splinter and the beam — you’ve got a lumberyard.
response: “There’s a line,” he says. “Matthew. A guy’s worried about the splinter in his brother’s eye, and there’s a beam in his own. A wooden *beam*. That’s the actual word.” He puts his mouth by her ear. “Skye. I’ve got a lumberyard.”
She laughs into her knees.
“I could build you a house out of what’s in my eye,” he says. “Two stories. A porch.”
“That leans,” she says, into the flannel, and under his arms the stiffness goes out of her back a little at a time.
“You’re the only person who’s ever told me no and meant it,” Skye says. “Do you know what that does to a person?”
He doesn’t. He holds on.

She turns around inside his arms at last, flannel and cuffs and all, and puts her face in his neck. “I thought you’d hug me and not answer,” she says there. “That’s what nice people do. They hold you so they don’t have to say it.”
And she leans.

choices.text: Tell her about your brother.
choices.key: At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and told her you’ve never thought less of your brother for a minute.
response: “My brother’s in prison,” he says. “I’ve never thought less of him for one minute. Not one.” He can feel his own heart going against her back. “He’s the best person in my family. I’d say it in front of anybody.”
“Me, I don’t let off for anything. That’s about the right way round.”
“You talk about him like he’s the good one,” Skye says.
“He is.”
She’s quiet. One of her hands comes out of its cuff and finds his wrist and holds on to it.
“You’re the only person who’s ever told me no and meant it,” Skye says. “Do you know what that does to a person?”
He doesn’t. He holds on.

She turns around inside his arms at last, flannel and cuffs and all, and puts her face in his neck. “I thought you’d hug me and not answer,” she says there. “That’s what nice people do. They hold you so they don’t have to say it.”
And she leans.

choices.text: Give her Lewis.
choices.key: At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and gave her C. S. Lewis on loving the sinner — easy on everybody, hard on yourself.
response: “C. S. Lewis has a thing,” he says.
“Who’s Lewis?”
“Narnia.”
“The *lion*?”
“The lion.”
“Fine. I trust the lion.”

“About hating what somebody does and not hating them,” he says. “He thought it was straw-splitting for years. Then he noticed there was one man he’d been doing it to all his life.” He’s known it since he was fifteen. “*However much I might dislike my own cowardice or conceit or greed, I went on loving myself.* He says there was never the slightest difficulty about it. That’s the trick. You do that for everybody.”
Into her hair: “Lewis says that part comes easy. I’ve got it backwards. Everybody else, easy. Me, I can’t do it.”
“You’re a mess, Jack,” Skye says, into the flannel.
“I’ve heard.”
“You’re the only person who’s ever told me no and meant it,” Skye says. “Do you know what that does to a person?”
He doesn’t. He holds on.

She turns around inside his arms at last, flannel and cuffs and all, and puts her face in his neck. “I thought you’d hug me and not answer,” she says there. “That’s what nice people do. They hold you so they don’t have to say it.”
And she leans.

s19a.slug: FRIDAY · 4:15 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: At a quarter past four he’s sitting against the wall at the head of the bed and she’s against him, her back to his chest in the flannel, his arms where they were. Past the lights the window hasn’t got anything in it yet. At the foot of the bluff, a long way under the house, the surf comes in slow and goes out slower, and the party three houses down has finally given up and gone to bed.
She’s drawing on his forearm with one fingernail: letters he can’t read, or a map, or nothing.
“What time does the sun come up?” she says. “In December.”
“Ten to seven. Around there.”
“I’ve only ever seen it from a makeup chair.”
“How many candles now?” she says. “On your thing.”
“Two. The third one’s Sunday. That one’s pink.”
“*Pink*?”
“Rose. It’s the rejoicing one.”
“You people have a color for *rejoicing*.” She thinks about that. “What’s the color for this?”
He doesn’t know. Purple, probably. The waiting one.
The fingernail goes on. “Are you going to tell your priest about tonight?”
“Yes.”
“What’ll you say?”
“That I came here. That I wanted to. That I said no.”
“Do you get points for the no?”
“It doesn’t work like points.”
“Everything works like points.” She thinks. “Will he know it’s me?”
“He won’t know your name. And nothing that goes in there comes back out. That’s the deal.”
“Good deal,” she says.
The fingernail stops. “So tell me the rules,” Skye says, into his shirt. “I always want the rules. Is that it? Forever? Till some man in a robe says the words?”
She asks it the way she’d ask a director what the scene is, before she has to go and play it.
He could say forever. It’s the right answer, and it would come out of him sounding like a vow he hasn’t got, and she’d hear that; she hears everything.

He knows what he was like at the turnout, and in the trailer, and here on this mattress at twenty past eleven. He isn’t going to promise her a man he isn’t sure of. And at half past three she asked him if he thought she was a slut, and he wants, more than he wants to be right, to be kind.

“I’m not saying the answer’s always going to be no,” he says. “Not until marriage — I’m not going to tell you that. I don’t know that about me.” Her hair is under his chin. “Just that it’s a big thing for me. And it’s a no right now.”
“I can work with that,” Skye says.
She says it right away, pleased, and he feels her smile against his shirt.

choices.text: “You’re going to be cruel about this.”
choices.key: At four in the morning you told her it’s a no right now — not always, not until marriage, just now. She said she can work with that. You told her she was going to be cruel about it.
response: “You’re going to be cruel about this.”
“Cruel’s a strong word,” Skye says. “I’m going to be *thorough*.”
He laughs, and she lies there against him being pleased with the word, and says it once more to herself, trying the weight of it, and keeps it.
“You’re going to be sorry you gave me that one,” she says.
“I know.”

She slides down the mattress and puts her head on his knee in the flannel, and he puts his hand on her hair. Her eyes are shut. She tells him about January with them shut: this room, with the window fixed and the other half of the lights working; the classes she hasn’t picked; a bicycle she’s going to buy and be bad at, in daylight, where everybody can see; a backpack, a real one, with a water bottle in the side. She has never owned a backpack. Her voice gets slower around the bicycle and doesn’t quite make it to the end of the backpack.
She has never had anybody stay this late, she says, who wasn’t being paid to.

choices.text: “I meant it as a no.”
choices.key: At four in the morning you told her it’s a no right now — not always, not until marriage, just now. She said she can work with that. You told her you meant it as a no.
response: “I meant it as a no.”
“I know,” Skye says. “I heard the whole sentence.” She taps his chest once, on *whole*.

“Both halves,” she says. “I always learn both halves. It’s how you don’t get fired.” She settles her head against him. “*No* is the first half. I heard it. I’m not deaf, Jack. I’m just very good at the second half.”

She slides down the mattress and puts her head on his knee in the flannel, and he puts his hand on her hair. Her eyes are shut. She tells him about January with them shut: this room, with the window fixed and the other half of the lights working; the classes she hasn’t picked; a bicycle she’s going to buy and be bad at, in daylight, where everybody can see; a backpack, a real one, with a water bottle in the side. She has never owned a backpack. Her voice gets slower around the bicycle and doesn’t quite make it to the end of the backpack.
She has never had anybody stay this late, she says, who wasn’t being paid to.

choices.text: Say nothing. She’s already smiling at the ceiling.
choices.key: At four in the morning you told her it’s a no right now — not always, not until marriage, just now. She said she can work with that. You let it stand.
response: He lets it stand. She has tipped her head back against his shoulder and is smiling at the ceiling.
“Right now,” she says, to the Christmas lights, like a woman writing a date in a book.
She says it again a minute later, quieter, to herself.

She tells him about January with them shut: this room, with the window fixed and the other half of the lights working; the classes she hasn’t picked; a bicycle she’s going to buy and be bad at, in daylight, where everybody can see; a backpack, a real one, with a water bottle in the side. She has never owned a backpack. Her voice gets slower around the bicycle and doesn’t quite make it to the end of the backpack.
She has never had anybody stay this late, she says, who wasn’t being paid to.

s20.slug: FRIDAY · 5:40 AM · DEL PLAYA, THE PORCH THAT LEANS
body: At twenty to six the sky over the Grove isn’t gray yet, only a black a shade lighter than the rest, with the eucalyptus standing up against it in a ragged row. Cloud is coming in off the water, and low in the east, in a gap it hasn’t closed, there’s a crescent of moon as thin as a paring. Somewhere down Del Playa a sprinkler is working at a lawn in the dark and hitting the sidewalk every third pass. A gull goes over, complaining. The party three houses down has turned into a porch light and a lawn full of cups.

She walks him out onto the porch in the flannel and his Carhartt, which she took down off the hook over the dress on the way out of her room and put on. It comes to the middle of her thighs, and she has the cuffs turned back twice. The boards lean toward the street. She’s used to the lean; he puts a hand on the post. He’s tired enough that the porch seems to lean more than it does. Her feet are bare on the boards, and she stands one on top of the other to keep half of them warm.

A car goes by slow with its window down and a newspaper comes out of it in a plastic sleeve and lands on the lawn next door, and the car goes on to the next one. A few drops come down on the porch roof and quit, like the weather hasn’t decided.
“The boys come back Sunday,” she says, looking at the empty rack. “They’ll want to know who you were.”
“What’ll you tell them?”
“My cousin from Ohio.”

She looks down Del Playa at the cups on the lawn and the sprinkler and the newspapers in their sleeves, at Las Olas asleep in every direction. “I like it at this hour,” she says. “Everybody’s too asleep to want anything.”

At the top of the steps she takes the Carhartt off and holds it out to him by the collar, and doesn’t let go of it yet. Her face in the porch dark is tired and scrubbed and very young, and her mouth is a little swollen, and so, he’d bet, is his.
“You said no,” Skye says. “And you’re still here.”

choices.text: “I’m still here.”
choices.key: At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You said: I’m still here.
response: “I’m still here,” Jack says.
She sits down on the top step in the flannel and holds the Carhartt up by one sleeve while he gets his arm into it, and the other. “Go,” she says, “before I ask you to stay. The sleeping way.”
“Is there a sleeping way?”
“I’ve never tried it.”
She lets go of the sleeve. He goes down the steps, and at the sidewalk he looks back, and she’s still sitting there on the top step with her feet tucked up under the flannel, watching him go.

choices.text: Go now, while she’s still smiling.
choices.key: At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You went while she was still smiling.
response: He takes the jacket out of her hand and puts it on and kisses her once, on the top step, quick, while she’s still smiling. “Go on, then,” she says, and gives him a small shove in the chest, and he goes down the steps. At the sidewalk he turns east. She watches him to the corner; he can feel it between his shoulder blades the length of the block. He doesn’t look back.

choices.text: “Meet me somewhere. In daylight.”
choices.key: At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You asked her to meet you somewhere in daylight.
response: “Meet me somewhere,” he says. “In daylight.”

She laughs at him on the porch at a quarter to six, and the gull on the roof next door answers her. “You’ve *had* daylight. You had me Thursday.” She holds the jacket up and he gets into it. “Sunday,” she says. “Ellery. I’ll teach you to surf. In *December*.” She zips him up to the chin like a mother at a bus stop. “That’s my daylight.”

s20e.slug: FRIDAY · 5:52 AM · DEL PLAYA, THE CORNER
body: At the corner where Del Playa meets the lane up to campus he takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt and holds the red key down. It wakes into the empty street with its little rising chord, and puts 5:52 on the outer screen, and hunts for a bar, and finds one, and buzzes once in his hand.

body.text: You left in the second chorus.
Thank you for staying. He said you told him. —L.

body: That’s the only one. Nothing after it, from her or from anybody.
Back down the block a screen door bangs, once, and the street goes quiet again.

He reads it at the corner with the light coming up gray at last behind the eucalyptus. He doesn’t answer it. He puts the phone back in the pocket of the Carhartt, which smells of her room now — mint tea and Sharpie and whatever she puts in her hair — and walks east toward campus between two fences of jasmine gone over for the year. At the edge of the Grove the eucalyptus has got the wet into it already and smells like a medicine cabinet. He goes in under it with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and the first of the rain starting, small and cold, on the back of his neck.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom and no surfboards — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that.
